**Course source:** Day 4 §1.1–§1.2. **Running example:** a shop with Product, Order and User services.

## The limitation of synchronous calls

Order can call Product and User synchronously to validate a checkout. But sending an order confirmation email does not necessarily need to block the customer until email delivery completes. The course introduces messaging to reduce this tight timing dependency.

~~~text
Order -> event "order.placed" -> broker -> Notification consumer
                                      -> Analytics consumer
~~~

A **producer** publishes a message to a logical destination; a **consumer** processes it. A broker manages transport and delivery. Messaging changes when components interact, not merely the syntax of their methods.

## Why Stream has a binder

RabbitMQ talks about exchanges and queues; Kafka talks about topics, partitions and consumer groups. The course introduces a **Binder** that maps framework-level channels/destinations onto broker-specific primitives.

This abstraction can reduce application coupling to a broker. It does **not** make all brokers semantically identical: acknowledgement, ordering, redelivery, partition assignment and retention still vary.

## Minimal business event

~~~json
{
  "type": "order.placed",
  "orderId": 42,
  "userId": 9,
  "productId": 7,
  "occurredAt": "2026-11-18T00:00:00Z"
}
~~~

The timestamp above illustrates an event shape, not a real order. Event schemas need versioning and stable identifiers so consumers can evolve independently.

## Correctness before scalability

A producer can crash after saving an order but before publishing its event. A consumer can process an event and crash before acknowledging it. These failure windows motivate the **transactional outbox**, idempotent consumers and explicit delivery semantics.

The small lab emits an in-process EventEmitter event. That is useful pedagogically but **not durable, distributed messaging**.

## Current Spring Cloud Stream direction

The supplied PDFs use historical annotation/channel patterns. Modern Spring Cloud Stream recommends a **functional** model based on Supplier, Function and Consumer rather than the older EnableBinding/StreamListener style.

[Spring Cloud Stream reference](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-stream/reference/).

## Questions to answer aloud

What problem does this design solve? Which guarantee does it give, and which guarantee does it **not** give? How would you detect incorrect operation?
